# fCWTr

The R package fCWTr wraps the [fCWT
library](https://github.com/fastlib/fCWT), a library implementing a
[continuous wavelet
transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_wavelet_transform)
with a Morlet wavelet, utilizing the power of
[fftw](https://www.fftw.org/), a fast fourier transform implementation.
It provides an R-like functional interface and implements common S3
methods for convenience.

See the original paper by Arts, L.P.A., van den Broek, E.L. The fast
continuous wavelet transformation (fCWT) for real-time, high-quality,
noise-resistant time–frequency analysis. Nat Comput Sci 2, 47–58 (2022).
<https://doi.org/10.1038/s43588-021-00183-z>

## System dependencies

- R \>= 4.1
- [fftw](https://www.fftw.org/) library with [single-precision
  support](https://www.fftw.org/faq/section2.html#singleprec) enabled
  (used by [fCWT](https://github.com/fastlib/fCWT))
- Optional: a CPU/compiler supporting the
  [AVX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Vector_Extensions)
  instruction set
- Optional: OpenMP (and fftw built with [OpenMP
  support](https://www.fftw.org/doc/Usage-of-Multi_002dthreaded-FFTW.html))
  - On Windows, OpenMP support is disabled since rtools’ fftw is
    compiled without OpenMP support.
  - On Linux and MacOS the build scripts should automatically detect
    whether OpenMP support is available.

By default, most compiler setups do not make use of AVX to increase
portability of the binary. If you are an R user that has a CPU
supporting AVX and want to make use of it, you might need to manually
enable compiler flags to let R know about it, and install the package
from source (so that it gets compiled on your machine). One way to
enable the flags is to create a file `~/.R/Makevars` with the following
content:

``` bash
CPPFLAGS = -mavx
CXXFLAGS = -mavx
```

## Installation

You can install the latest CRAN release of fCWTr with:

``` r

install.packages("fCWTr")
```

Alternatively, you can install the development version of fCWTr like so
(requiring installed [devtools](https://devtools.r-lib.org/) package):

``` r

devtools::install_github("lschneiderbauer/fCWTr")
```

Note that the installation process might fail if the package needs to be
compiled from source and system requirements are not satisfied. The
error message should give you hints, however, on what’s missing on your
system.

- Common confusion: fftw is installed, but without single precision
  support (`libfftw3f`). Some distributions ship it as a separate
  package:
  - Debian/Ubuntu: `libfftw3-dev`
  - Fedora/RHEL: `fftw-devel` and `fftw-libs-single`
  - macOS: `brew install fftw` (or the CRAN macOS recipe `fftw-s`)
  - If you build fftw yourself, configure it with `--enable-float`. See
    [fftw.org](https://www.fftw.org/faq/section2.html#singleprec).

## Example

This is a basic example where the continuous wavelet transform of a
sample signal is calculated. The result is inspected and plotted.

``` r

library(fCWTr)

# A signal encoded in a numeric vector.
# In this example we use some superimposed sin signals.
signal <- ts_sin_superpos

output <-
  fcwt(
    signal,
    x_sample_freq = u(44.1, "kHz"),
    sigma = 5,
    y_sample_freq = u(1, "kHz"),
    freq_begin = u(16, "Hz"),
    freq_end = u(2100, "Hz"),
    n_freqs = 200,
    freq_scale = "linear"
  )

# The result is a numeric matrix with time and frequency dimension
dim(output)
#> [1] 137 200

# Some meta data is recorded too
output
#> _Scalogram_
#> * (Time/Frequency) dimension:  ( 137 , 200 )
#> * Sampling rate: 1 [kHz]
#> * Frequency scale: 16 [Hz] - 2100 [Hz], linear
#> * Time offset: 0 [s] 
#> * Sigma: 5
#>   o Time resolution at  16 [Hz] :  1.25 [1/Hz] 
#>   o Time resolution at  2100 [Hz] :  0.00952381 [1/Hz] 
#>   o Relative frequency resolution:  0.127324 
#> * Time/frequency matrix summary
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
#>   0.000   0.000   0.000   0.003   0.001   0.064    6671
```

The result can also be converted into a data frame:

``` r

as.data.frame(output) |>
  head(10)
#>    time_index      time      freq        value
#> 1           0 0.000 [s] 2100 [Hz]           NA
#> 2           1 0.001 [s] 2100 [Hz]           NA
#> 3           2 0.002 [s] 2100 [Hz]           NA
#> 4           3 0.003 [s] 2100 [Hz]           NA
#> 5           4 0.004 [s] 2100 [Hz] 5.170488e-05
#> 6           5 0.005 [s] 2100 [Hz] 2.023599e-05
#> 7           6 0.006 [s] 2100 [Hz] 7.007858e-06
#> 8           7 0.007 [s] 2100 [Hz] 2.413503e-06
#> 9           8 0.008 [s] 2100 [Hz] 1.058135e-06
#> 10          9 0.009 [s] 2100 [Hz] 6.853825e-07
```

We can also directly plot the resulting scalogram:

``` r

plot(output, time_unit = "ms")
```

![](reference/figures/README-example_plot-1.png)

For long sequences, the required memory can exceed your available local
memory. In this case it can be useful to reduce the time resolution of
the result and process the data in batches. This can be done with
[`fcwt_batch()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/fcwt_batch.md).
In case the batch size is not explicitly provided, some heuristics are
used to determine a batch size automatically:

``` r

batch_result <-
  fcwt_batch(
    rep(ts_sin_sin, 5),
    x_sample_freq = u(44.1, "kHz"),
    y_sample_freq = u(100, "Hz"),
    freq_begin = u(100, "Hz"),
    freq_end = u(12, "kHz"),
    n_freqs = 200,
    freq_scale = "linear",
    sigma = 4
  )

plot(batch_result)
```

![](reference/figures/README-example_long_df-1.png)

# Package index

## Fast continuous wavelet transform

Functions for performing fast continuous wavelet transforms. These
constitue the core functionality of this package.

- [`fcwt()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/fcwt.md)
  : Fast continuous wavelet transform
- [`fcwt_batch()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/fcwt_batch.md)
  : Fast continuous wavelet transform - Batch processing

## Sigma helpers

Helpers to setup the correct wavelet spread parameter sigma.

- [`sigma_freq_res_rel()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/sigma_freq_res_rel.md)
  : Calculates Relative Frequency Resolution
- [`sigma_from_freq_res()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/sigma_from_freq_res.md)
  : Determine Sigma from a frequency resolution requirement
- [`sigma_from_freq_res_rel()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/sigma_from_freq_res_rel.md)
  : Determine Sigma from a relative frequency resolution requirement
- [`sigma_from_time_res()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/sigma_from_time_res.md)
  : Determine Sigma from a time resolution requirement
- [`sigma_res()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/sigma_res.md)
  : Calculates Time/Frequency Resolution

## Physical unit helper

- [`u()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/u.md) :
  Augment physical unit
- [`du()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/du.md) :
  Drop physical unit

## Scalogram S3 methods

A data.frame conversion method, data extractors, and optional ggplot2
plotting methods (they only work if ggplot is installed).

- [`as.data.frame(`*`<fcwtr_scalogram>`*`)`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/as.data.frame.fcwtr_scalogram.md)
  : Convert the scalogram matrix to a data frame
- [`as_tibble(`*`<fcwtr_scalogram>`*`)`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/as_tibble.fcwtr_scalogram.md)
  : Convert the scalogram matrix to a tibble
- [`as.matrix(`*`<fcwtr_scalogram>`*`)`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/as.matrix.fcwtr_scalogram.md)
  : Extract the data matrix from a scalogram
- [`` `[`( ``*`<fcwtr_scalogram>`*`)`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/sub-.fcwtr_scalogram.md)
  : Extract parts of a scalogram
- [`rbind(`*`<fcwtr_scalogram>`*`)`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/rbind.fcwtr_scalogram.md)
  : Combine scalograms in "time" direction
- [`print(`*`<fcwtr_scalogram>`*`)`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/print.fcwtr_scalogram.md)
  : Print the scalogram
- [`plot(`*`<fcwtr_scalogram>`*`)`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/plot.fcwtr_scalogram.md)
  : Scalogram plotting
- [`autoplot(`*`<fcwtr_scalogram>`*`)`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/autoplot.fcwtr_scalogram.md)
  : Create a ggplot object resembling a scalogram

## System support

Helper functions that let you check if your platform provides OpenMP or
AVX support.

- [`avx_enabled()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/avx_enabled.md)
  : Check for AVX instruction set support
- [`openmp_enabled()`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/openmp_enabled.md)
  : Check for OpenMP support

## Sample data

Sample signal data mainly used to generate examples. The signals consist
of simple superpositions of sinusoidal patterns.

- [`ts_piano_sample`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/ts_piano_sample.md)
  : A simple piano audio sample
- [`ts_sin_440`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/ts_sin_440.md)
  : Pure sine wave
- [`ts_sin_sin`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/ts_sin_sin.md)
  : A sinusoidal wave with varying frequency
- [`ts_sin_superpos`](https://lschneiderbauer.github.io/fCWTr/reference/ts_sin_superpos.md)
  : Superimposed sine waves of different frequencies and different
  amplitudes
